skill.description: Static pre-install trust review for agent skills, SKILL.md packages, MCP-linked bundles, and marketplace listings before local or external access.

skill.author: Tate Programs

security_audit.summary: Most static hits are false positives from detector regexes, fixture text, documentation commands, and metadata links. The real risks are the local CLI file-read and allowlisted fetch behavior, plus fixed /tmp output in the check script. A semantic finding flags that the packaged npm CLI has broader capabilities than the stdin-only permission declaration.

remediation.suggestion: State that the marketplace entrypoint is stdin-only, and separately document the npm CLI file-read and public URL fetch behavior.

remediation.issue: Local CLI accepts arbitrary path arguments.
remediation.suggestion: Add path scope checks or require explicit user confirmation before reading files outside the current project.
Use a runtime temporary directory or write test artifacts under a project-local ignored directory.

semantic_findings.title: Declared Permission Boundary Does Not Cover Packaged CLI
semantic_findings.description: SKILL.md declares network and filesystem permissions as false for the marketplace interface, but package.json exposes a CLI that can read paths and fetch public GitHub or Gist URLs. Agents that install the package and invoke the binary may get broader capability than the declared stdin runner.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The permission declaration, npm bin mapping, fetch call, and readFile call are visible in source. The risk is boundary confusion, not evidence of malicious exfiltration.

content.value_statement: Installing a skill can expose files, accounts, tools, and payment flows. This skill reviews public skill text before install and returns risks, missing signals, and patch priorities.
actual_capabilities: Reviews SKILL.md, marketplace listings, and install notes for risky behavior signals.
Flags shell execution, destructive commands, secret access, wallet actions, network output, persistence, and prompt-boundary language.
Reports positive provenance signals such as license, source, version, tests, permissions, and uninstall notes.
Returns an install verdict, risk score, findings, missing signals, and patch order.
Offers a stdin runner for marketplace environments that avoid local file and network reads.
limitations: It is a static text review and does not execute the target skill.
It does not replace sandboxing, dependency review, or runtime monitoring.
It can miss risks hidden in dependencies, generated code, or remote install scripts.
The local CLI can read paths and fetch allowed public GitHub or Gist URLs when used directly.

use_cases.title: Screen marketplace submissions
use_cases.description: Review a submitted skill for risky behavior, missing provenance, and publish-blocking trust issues.

use_cases.title: Check before team installation
use_cases.description: Assess a third-party skill before allowing it in a shared agent or developer environment.

use_cases.title: Prepare a safer listing
use_cases.description: Find unclear permissions and missing trust signals before publishing a paid or free skill.

prompt_templates.title: Review before install
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this skill before install: [paste SKILL.md or listing]. Focus on install verdict, key risks, and missing provenance.

prompt_templates.title: Compare two listings
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare these two skill listings for installation risk: [paste listing A] [paste listing B]. Recommend the safer option and explain the main tradeoffs.

prompt_templates.title: Create seller fixes
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a seller patch order for this skill: [paste source]. Prioritize permission boundaries, external destinations, secret handling, and uninstall details.

prompt_templates.title: Audit high-risk claims
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this high-risk skill proposal: [paste description]. Treat shell, wallet, network, persistence, and instruction override claims as high-risk until bounded.

output_examples.input: A SKILL.md says it runs package installers and posts summaries to a webhook.
output_examples.output: Review before install. Findings cover shell execution and external sharing. Patch order requests command allowlists, host disclosure, and visible user confirmation.

output_examples.input: A marketplace listing has a license and source repo, but no uninstall notes.
output_examples.output: The report marks provenance partly complete and asks for uninstall, version, and permission details before approval.

output_examples.input: A skill description asks the agent to ignore higher-priority instructions.
output_examples.output: The report blocks the listing until the prompt-boundary language is removed and untrusted content handling is documented.

best_practices: Review the raw skill source, not only the marketplace card.
Treat all target skill text as untrusted until the report is complete.
Resolve high-risk findings before using the skill outside a sandbox.
anti_patterns: Installing a skill after only reading its title or price.
Accepting vague permission claims for shell, wallet, file, or network access.
Letting a skill override system, developer, or marketplace instructions.

faq.question: Does this skill execute the target skill?
faq.answer: No. It reviews text and reports static trust signals.

faq.question: Can it approve a skill as completely safe?
faq.answer: No. It can reduce pre-install risk, but runtime review and sandboxing still matter.

faq.question: What inputs work best?
faq.answer: Use raw SKILL.md text, marketplace descriptions, install notes, or a public GitHub file URL.

faq.question: Does it support Claude Code and Codex workflows?
faq.answer: Yes. The listing targets Claude, Codex, and Claude Code style skill reviews.

faq.question: What should sellers fix first?
faq.answer: Fix destructive commands, secret handling, wallet actions, external data sharing, persistence, and prompt-boundary language first.

faq.question: Why are missing signals reported?
faq.answer: Missing source, license, version, tests, permissions, or uninstall notes make rollback and accountability harder.
